what: Says engagement 'can lead to' more antagonistic and hostile interactions. The paper says engagement 'may also be associated with' antagonistic behavior and that its evidence 'does not establish that engagement causes hostility' (p.15).

Says the paper contests the notion that affective polarization is 'merely a byproduct of hostility' and suggests it 'may be a key driver'. The paper argues against no such view; it treats leader-directed affective polarization as a possible condition of the engagement-hostility association and says it 'may be an antecedent, correlate, or consequence' of hostile interaction (p.14).
Says broader polarization and elite influence 'must also be addressed'. The paper says reducing hostility 'may also require attention to' broader polarization and the role of elites (p.16).
Says the paper argues against the idea that hostility is 'a sign of disengagement or extremism'. The paper attributes no such view to anyone.

Uses Almond and Verba's 'active, yet passive' passage to say the paper opposes the view that engagement leads to passive, disengaged citizens. Almond and Verba said engagement should be tempered ('involved, yet not too involved'), and the paper builds on that point (p.4); it opposes no such view.

Says engagement 'may be a key driver of polarization and conflict'. The paper reports associations with hostility, not that engagement drives polarization; it lists engagement increasing affective polarization only as one possible reciprocal pathway (p.16) and disclaims causal claims.

Says the paper disputes the view that political engagement is primarily driven by socioeconomic status or education. The paper treats education as a distal antecedent of engagement (p.4) and disputes no such view.

Says the paper argues against the idea that engagement leads to disengagement and that engagement 'increases visibility and reach through hostile behavior'. The paper argues against no such view and reports only that more hostile users post more and have more friends and followers, suggesting greater potential reach, 'exploratory and descriptive' (p.15).

Says the paper disputes the claim that political engagement is limited to offline activities. The paper attributes no such claim to anyone; it measures online and offline participation separately (p.9).

Says the paper challenges the idea that hostility is primarily driven by psychological traits and links it to 'structural and contextual factors'. The paper does not adjudicate between the literatures (p.3) and links hostility to political engagement, not to structural or contextual factors.

Says the paper argues against the idea that engagement is limited to educated or well-informed citizens and that it is 'accessible and widespread'. The paper says nothing of the kind; the quote is about social media lowering entry barriers to the public sphere (p.1).
Says the paper disputes the claim that engagement is limited to structured civic participation. The paper disputes no such claim; it simply measures online and offline participation (p.9).

Says the paper challenges the idea that engagement is 'only beneficial for political knowledge' and shows it is linked to 'affective and behavioral indicators'. Nothing in the paper corresponds to this.

Says the paper argues against the view that political engagement is a 'simple or linear process'. The paper attributes no such view to anyone; it notes only that the engagement-hostility relationship may be reciprocal and that affective polarization and engagement may affect each other (p.15-16).
Says the paper challenges the view that political engagement is limited to specific parties or ideologies. The paper says nothing of the kind.
Says the paper argues against the notion that political engagement is a solitary or private activity. The paper attributes no such notion to anyone.

Calls the hesitancy measures 'validated scales'. The paper modified the AAVS items for COVID-19 and took booster items from a 2022 survey; it reports only that the modified items 'demonstrated adequate reliability' after a CFA (p.5), never that the scales are validated.

'The counter-narrative significantly increases positive perceptions' drops that it was shown before the ad and is compared with the ad alone; there was no counter-narrative-only arm (p.16). The quote keeps the qualification.

Says the paper extends social categorization theory by incorporating perspective-getting. The paper grounds the counter-narrative in separate perspective-getting and counter-stereotype research (p.3, p.15); it does not present it as an extension of social categorization theory.

Says the paper disputes a claim that stigmatizing messaging increases support for punitive policies. The cited finding (p.2, [11]) is that anger toward people with records is associated with support for punitive policy, and the paper uses it as support for its concern, not something it disputes.
Says such messaging 'reduces feelings of representation'. The paper finds the ad improved perceived representation (p.1, p.11, p.15).

Frames the question as engagement 'rather than being primarily driven by' marginalization, personality or grievance. The paper asks whether hostility is associated 'not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement' (p.2) and does not adjudicate between those literatures (p.3).

Lists 'online/offline participation' among the strongest associations. The paper names political interest, political knowledge and online participation (p.1); offline participation is not among the strongest.
Says the controls 'isolate the effect of political engagement indicators on hostility'. The paper reports associations after controls and interprets them as 'associational rather than causal' (p.16).
Includes offline participation among the strongest associations. The paper names political interest, political knowledge and online participation (p.1).

Says the association between engagement and hostility is stronger for participatory indicators than for distal antecedents such as education. The paper says this of the moderation evidence (formal interaction models, p.13-14), not of the main association, whose strongest indicators are interest, knowledge and online participation (p.1).
Says the paper argues engagement 'may also lead to' antagonistic and polarized behavior. The paper says engagement 'may also be associated with' such behavior (p.1) and disclaims causal claims.

Says the paper builds on the biased-processing literature 'by showing that such patterns are especially pronounced in online political contexts and among politically engaged users'. The paper shows no such comparison; it reports that online hostility is associated with engagement indicators.

Says vaccine and booster hesitancy were both measured with the modified Attitudes towards Adult Vaccination Scale. The paper uses the AAVS for vaccine hesitancy only; booster hesitancy 'was assessed using items from a 2022 survey on COVID-19 booster hesitancy' (p.3).

Speaks of the mechanisms 'through which political climate affects booster uptake in conservatives', presupposing an effect. The paper says environmental factors 'may impact' annual doses and that it 'cannot assume causal or directional associations' (p.10). 'Peer influence' as an example is not in the paper.

Says the paper shows 'that liberal environments have a stronger influence on conservative individuals'. The paper only says the interaction 'suggests that liberal environments may exert more influence' and offers an alternative reading (conservatives more influenced by environments), and states it cannot assume causal or directional associations (p.10).

'The stigmatizing label led to a significant decrease' attributes the effect to the label; the stimulus was the mugshot with the label, and the paper says the two cannot be disentangled (p.17). The quote says 'the Trump advertisement'.
Says the counter-narrative increased perceptions by 0.83 SD without saying it preceded the ad and is compared with the ad alone (p.11, p.16). The quote keeps the qualification.
Says the ad increased perceived self-interest motives of officials; the paper finds the ad increased belief that officials are motivated by public service (p.11, beta = 0.130; p.15).
Says the ad reduced perceived quality of Democratic representation; the ad increased it (p.11, p.15). The decrease the quote reports is the counter-narrative's, relative to the ad alone (F5).
Says the counter-narrative increased perceived complexity of representation. H1E was unsupported: no significant difference, and the estimate is negative (-0.062, p.11).
Says exposure to the ad increased support for the advertisement. No such comparison exists: ad support was asked only after exposure to the ad in every arm and is not in Table 3 (p.10-11).

Says the counter-narrative 'reduced the negative perception of the quality of Democratic representation', i.e. improved it. The counter-narrative decreased perceived quality relative to the ad alone (p.11, beta = -0.332), as the quote says.

Says the counter-narrative reduced perceived self-interest motives of officials. It reduced belief that officials serve the public (p.11, beta = -0.098), as the quote says; the result also would not survive Bonferroni (F11).

Says prior work (ref. 94) found a strong negative correlation between conspiracy theories and polarization in Canada, which the paper disputes. Ref. 94 found reduced negative sentiment in Canadian vaccine tweets during 2020 (p.24); the paper contrasts that with its own null conspiracy correlation.

The note says the paper challenges the view that risky behaviors serve as a basis for peer identification in diverse school settings; the paper accepts that pattern for heterogeneous schools (p.4) and disputes only its generalization to AI-majority schools.
The note says responses were 'verified by trained research team members'; the paper says trained team members administered the survey (p.6) and mentions no verification.

The note calls degree-related effects 'strong and consistent drivers' along with reciprocity and transitivity; the paper says degree effects 'were more varied' (indegree significant only in School C, p.13). It also labels the descriptive transitivity levels (31.0-36.5%) as 'significant transitivity'.

The note says the AI identity null is 'because' nearly all students share the same racial background; the paper says the null 'is consistent with several contextual considerations' and offers this as the first of three.

The note says the study 'does not generalize' to AI youth in heterogeneous or urban schools; the paper says its findings 'may not extend' to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools (p.16) and does not mention urban schools.

The note says the paper disputes the substance-use claim by 'challenging the findings of Rees, Freng, and Winfree'; Rees et al. reported fewer reciprocated friendships among AI adolescents, not a substance-use link, and the paper builds on them, noting only that their analysis was descriptive (p.2) and citing their different findings in heterogeneous schools as a limit on generalization (p.16).

Says the association is stronger among the more affectively polarized, 'particularly for indicators of direct participation'. The paper says this holds for some indicators, is clearest for participation and is only 'partially consistent with Expectation 2' (p.14); the 'particularly' keeps part of the qualification.

Describes the revisionist view as saying engagement 'may lead to' biased and antagonistic behavior. The paper says engaged citizens 'may also be more likely to process information in biased or antagonistic ways' (p.2).

Says stigmatizing messaging can 'reduce public support for justice system reform'. The study measures no policy support, and the paper stresses that policy support is distinct from perceptions of the people affected (p.3).
Says the messaging may backfire by 'reducing feelings of representation'. The ad improved perceived representation (p.1, p.15).

Says stigmatizing messaging may 'reduce perceived public service motivation among elected officials'. The ad increased belief that officials are motivated by public service (p.11, p.15), as the entry's own quote says.
Says the messaging may create affective polarization. The paper cites the affective-polarization literature as a possible rationale for the ad (p.3) and does not measure polarization.

Says the paper argues stigmatizing rhetoric may deepen barriers to civic participation and turnout among system-impacted people. The paper says the counter-narrative approach 'may have been more strategic' given low turnout (p.18) and that the strategy 'may have facilitated even greater barriers to solidarity' (p.16); it reports no effect on participation.
Adds that such ads 'can have detrimental long-term effects on public trust'. Nothing in the paper says this; trust is not measured.

Says stigmatizing language 'may inadvertently reinforce systemic biases and deepen societal divisions'. The paper's nearest point is hedged and narrower: the strategy 'may have facilitated even greater barriers to solidarity amongst system-impacted constituents' (p.16), posed for future research (p.18).

Says the paper argues stigmatizing messaging may reduce empathy and political engagement. The paper measures neither; the quoted passage (p.3) is literature offered as a possible rationale for the ad, not an argument against it.

Says the paper argues stigmatizing language is ineffective for party loyalty because it may alienate voters. The paper raises a possible backfire 'though this is also not guaranteed' (p.3), and finds the ad improved perceived representation (p.15).

Says the paper argues against the idea that social media discourse is unrepresentative; the paper concedes Twitter data 'may not fully capture the views and sentiments of the broader American and Canadian public' and reflects 'a vocal subset' (p.24).

Says the paper argues that public health outcomes are influenced by the timing of policy announcements; the paper only reports that polarization peaks coincide with contentious events, noting 'direct causal evidence is not available' (p.17).
Says the paper argues polarization is a cause of social fragmentation; the paper says the high U.S. polarization levels 'indicate a more divided society' (p.23), not that polarization causes it.
The note calls sexual orientation homophily 'consistent'; the paper says only 'significant and positive' (p.13), and Table 3 shows it non-significant for one category in School B.

The note speaks of 'the absence of a significant association' for depression; the paper reports isolated statistically significant but negligible estimates (AME < 0.001, p.14). It also names 'withdrawal' among non-AI findings where the paper names negative receiver effects and homophily.
